title: Seven things I'm proud of
translation: The guard Chikatomo once wrote down seven things he was proud of. They're all about riding, and none of them is anything special. Following his example, here are seven of mine.

I was out looking at the cherry blossoms with a group of people, and near Saishōkō-in we saw a man galloping his horse. I said, "If he gallops that horse one more time, it'll go down and he'll come off. Wait and watch." We stopped, and he galloped it again. Just where he pulled up, he dragged the horse over, and the rider tumbled into the mud. Everyone was impressed that I'd called it right.

When the present emperor was still crown prince and living at the Madenokōji palace, I had some business with the Horikawa Grand Counsellor and went to his room there. He had the fourth, fifth and sixth scrolls of the Analects unrolled in front of him. "The crown prince wants to see the passage about hating purple for taking the place of red," he said. "He looked through his own copy and couldn't find it. He told me to look properly, so I'm looking." I said, "It's in the ninth scroll, about such-and-such a place." "Oh, wonderful!" he said, and took it in to the prince.

Any child could do that much. But people in the old days boasted about even the smallest things. Retired Emperor Go-Toba once asked Teika about a poem of his own: was it wrong to have both "sleeve" and "cuff", two words for nearly the same thing, in one poem? Teika answered that there was this old poem, so what could be wrong with it:

Is the pampas grass
the cuff of the grass
on the autumn fields?
Its plumes come out and wave
like a sleeve calling you over.

Even that little answer, he wrote down with great ceremony: "At the right moment I remembered the source poem. A blessing on my art, and great good luck." Koremichi, the Kujō chancellor, did the same. In a petition for promotion he listed things that were nothing special and praised himself for them.

The inscription for the bell at Jōzaikō-in was drafted by Arikane. Yukifusa had written out the fair copy, and they were about to have it cast, when the lay priest in charge got out the draft and showed it to me. One line went: "Beyond the blossoms it sees off the evening, and its sound carries a hundred miles." I said, "The lines seem to rhyme on -ang. Isn't 'a hundred miles' a mistake?" "I'm so glad I showed you," he said. "This is a feather in my cap." He sent word to the author, who wrote back: "It's a mistake. Change it to 'several rows'." I'm not sure about "several rows" either. Maybe it's meant as "a few paces"? I don't know.

I went with a group of people on a pilgrimage round the three precincts of Mount Hiei. In the Jōgyō Hall at Yokawa there was an old tablet that said "Ryūge-in". The hall monk told us, with a lot of ceremony, "There's a tradition that it was written either by Sukemasa or by Yukinari. It has never been settled." I said, "If it's Yukinari's, there will be writing on the back. If it's Sukemasa's, there won't." The back was thick with dust and insects' nests, a nasty sight, but they swept and wiped it clean, and we all looked. There were Yukinari's rank, his name and the year, perfectly clear. Everyone was delighted.

At Nārandaji, the priest Dōgen was giving a lecture and forgot the eight things that disturb meditation. "Does anyone remember them?" he asked. None of his students did. From the side room where I was sitting I called out, "Isn't it this, this and this?" They were very impressed.

I went with the senior priest Kenjo to watch the holy-water rite at the palace. He left before it was over, and outside the guard post one of his priests was nowhere to be seen. He sent his monks back in to look, but they took a very long time and came out saying, "There are too many monks dressed the same. We couldn't find him." "Oh, what a nuisance," he said to me. "You go and find him." I went back in and came straight out with him.

On the fifteenth night of mid-spring, the day the Buddha died, the moon was bright. Late at night I went to the temple at Senbon. I came in at the back and sat alone listening to the service, with my face well hidden. A lovely woman, whose looks and scent stood out from everyone, made her way through and sat leaning against my knee. Her scent was close to rubbing off on me. That was awkward, so I slid away. She moved up close again, the same as before, so I got up and left.

Some time later, an older lady-in-waiting from one of the palaces was chatting with me about nothing in particular, and she said, "We were rather disappointed in you. You have no romance in you at all. Someone is quite upset with you for being so cold." "I have no idea what you mean," I said, and that was that.

I heard later what had happened. That night at the service, someone in one of the curtained boxes had recognised me. They dressed up one of their ladies and sent her out: "If you get the chance, talk to him. Then come back and tell me how it went. It'll be fun." It was all a set-up.

literal: There is a thing where the guard Chikatomo wrote down seven items as his self-praise.
All of them are matters of horsemanship of no particular importance.
Thinking of that precedent, I have seven matters of self-praise.

Item: when I went about viewing blossoms with many people, near Saishōkō-in, seeing a man make his horse run, I said, 'If he gallops the horse once more, the horse will fall and he will drop off; watch for a while', and when we stopped, he galloped the horse again.
At the place where he reined in, he pulled the horse down, and the rider tumbled into the mud.
Everyone admired that my words had not been wrong.

Item: when the present emperor was still in the crown prince's quarters, the Madenokōji palace being his residence, when I went on business to the room where the Horikawa Grand Counsellor was in attendance, he had the fourth, fifth and sixth scrolls of the Analects unrolled, and
'Just now at the palace, (the prince) wished to see the passage that says (Confucius) hates purple taking the place of red, and looked in his book, but could not find it.

It is by his order that I should look again carefully, so I am searching,' he said, and when I said, 'It is around such-and-such a place in the ninth scroll', he said 'How glad I am!' and took it to (the prince).
Such a thing is ordinary even for children, but people of old boasted greatly of even trifling things.
About a poem of Retired Emperor Go-Toba, when he asked Lord Teika, 'Would it be bad to have sleeve and cuff in one poem?',
'Is it the cuff of the grass of the autumn fields, the flowering pampas grass, that, coming out in plumes, it looks like a sleeve beckoning?'

(Teika) said, 'Since there is this, what could be the matter?', and even that, he wrote down grandly: 'At the right time I remembered the source poem; it is the divine favour of the Way, it is great good fortune.'
In a petition of the Kujō chancellor, Lord Koremichi, too, he wrote down even items of no particular importance and praised himself.
Item: the inscription of the hanging bell of Jōzaikō-in was drafted by Lord Arikane.

When Yukifusa Ason had made the fair copy and they were about to have it transferred to the mould, the lay priest in charge took out that draft and showed it to me, and there was a line, 'Seeing off the evening beyond the blossoms, its voice is heard for a hundred li.'

When I said, 'It seems to be in the yang-tang rhyme; is "hundred li" a mistake?', he said, 'How well I did to show it to you. It is to my credit', and sent word to the writer, and the reply came: 'It was a mistake. It should be corrected to "several rows".'
What 'several rows' could mean, too: is it perhaps in the sense of 'several paces'? It is unclear.
Item: when I made a pilgrimage of the three pagodas with many people, in the Jōgyō Hall at Yokawa there was an old tablet with 'Ryūge-in' written on it.

When the hall monk said grandly, 'It has been handed down that there is doubt between Sukemasa and Yukinari, and it has not yet been settled', I said, 'If it is Yukinari, there should be writing on the back. If it is Sukemasa, there should be no writing on the back', and

the back was piled with dust and was an insects' nest, and was unpleasant, but they swept and wiped it well, and when each of us looked, Yukinari's rank and title, name and era name were clearly visible, so everyone was delighted.

Item: when the holy man Dōgen was giving a lecture at Nārandaji, he forgot the thing called the eight calamities and said, 'Does anyone remember?', and when none of the students remembered, from inside a compartment I said, 'Is it this and this?', and they were greatly impressed.
Item: when I went with Archbishop Kenjo to see the empowerment of holy water, before it had ended, the archbishop went back, and as far as outside the guard post the bishop could not be seen.

He sent the priests back to look for him, but they said, 'There are many monks of the same appearance, and we could not find him', and came out after a very long time; when he said, 'How annoying. You go and look for him', I went back in and soon came out bringing him.

Item: on the fifteenth of the second month, on a night with a bright moon, late at night I went to the temple at Senbon, entered from the back, and was listening alone with my face deeply hidden, when

a graceful woman, whose figure and scent were finer than others', made her way in and sat leaning onto my knee, so that even her scent was about to transfer, so I thought it awkward and slid away, but she moved closer again, and since it was the same, I stood up.
Afterwards, on the occasion of idle talk by a certain old lady-in-waiting of some palace: 'There was a time when we thought less of you, that you were a person utterly without romance.
There is a person who resents you as heartless,' she said, and I said, 'I do not understand at all', and it ended.

What I heard later about this: that night of the service, from inside a box, a person recognised me, dressed up a lady-in-waiting in their service and sent her out: 'If there is a good chance, speak words to him.
Come and tell me how it went; it will be amusing': they say it had been planned so.

notes.text: {随身|ずいじん}: a mounted guard of the court (see section 145). The 1925 edition says nothing is known of Chikatomo; modern commentaries identify him as Nakahara no Chikatomo, a guard and racing rider around 1100. {自讃|じさん}: 'praising oneself'. させる … なき: 'not particularly worth mentioning'. Kenkō says this of Chikatomo's list, and then writes one of his own.

A temple in the eastern outskirts of the capital (the 1925 edition: inside the grounds of Nanzenji). Modern commentaries place it near today's Sanjūsangendō instead, and note that it burned down in 1226 and was never rebuilt, so in Kenkō's day only the site was left. Compare section 145, where an expert in horses also sees a fall coming.

notes.quote: 当代いまだ坊におはしまししころ
notes.text: {当代|たうだい}: 'the present reign', Emperor Go-Daigo (the 1925 edition's gloss). He was crown prince from 1308 to 1318, so this passage at least was written while he was on the throne. {坊|ばう}: the crown prince's household, and so the crown prince himself.

The 1925 edition names Fujiwara no Moronobu, son of Morotsugu, then the crown prince's chief steward. Modern commentaries look to the Horikawa branch of the Minamoto instead, often Minamoto no Tomochika; the identification is not settled. {大納言|だいなごん}: Grand Counsellor, one of the highest posts below the ministers.

notes.quote: 紫の朱うばふ事を悪む
notes.text: From the Analects (book 17): Confucius hates the way purple takes the place of red. Red was the proper colour, purple a showy mixture, and the line is about the false pushing out the true (the 1925 edition: petty men overpowering the wise). In the ten-scroll editions used in Japan, book 17 is in the ninth scroll, not in the fourth to sixth that the counsellor was searching.

{袖|そで} and {袂|たもと} both mean the sleeve; たもと is more exactly the long hanging part of it. Go-Toba was worried about using two words for one thing. Teika (1162–1241) answered with a poem from the Kokinshū that has both, by Ariwara no Muneyana (so the 1925 edition and modern commentaries). The plumes of pampas grass waving in the wind were a standard image for a sleeve beckoning someone.

{本歌|ほんか}: 'the source poem', an older poem that a new one borrows from or leans on. {覚悟|かくご}: 'to remember, to have in mind' (the 1925 edition's gloss), not modern 'resolve'. {冥加|みやうが}: the unseen favour of the gods and buddhas, here of the gods of poetry (the 1925 edition: 'an honour for the way of poetry').

notes.quote: 九条相国伊通公の款状
notes.text: Fujiwara no Koremichi (1093–1165), who became Chancellor; {相国|しやうこく} is a Chinese-style name for the post (compare section 83). {款状|くわんじやう}: a written petition, usually for a post or promotion (the 1925 edition: 'a letter of request').

Jōzaikō-in was a temple in Higashiyama, in the east of the capital (the 1925 edition's gloss). Arikane is Sugawara no Arikane, of a family of scholars of Chinese. Yukifusa is Fujiwara no Yukifusa, a calligrapher of the Sesonji family of section 237. The inscription is in Chinese, so the 'hundred miles' is literally a hundred li, the Chinese mile.

{韻|ゐん}: rhyme. Chinese verse rhymes within fixed rhyme groups, and 陽 and 唐 name the group for words ending in -ang. The 1925 edition explains: the other lines end in that rhyme, but {里|り} belongs to a different group and a different tone. The correction {数行|すかう}, 'several rows', ends in 行 (hang), which does rhyme. Kenkō's new doubt is about what it would mean.
{高名|かうみやう}: 'a deed to be praised for', here a feather in the cap. おのれ is 'myself': the priest who thought of showing the draft counts it to his own credit.

notes.quote: 佐理・行成の間うたがひありて
notes.text: Fujiwara no Sukemasa (944–998) and Fujiwara no Yukinari (972–1028), who is also called Kōzei: two of the three great calligraphers of the Heian period (see section 25; the 1925 edition gives Sukemasa as the son of Atsutoshi). {裏書|うらがき}: writing on the back. The text does not say how Kenkō knew which of them signed their tablets. {位署|ゐしよ}: rank and title, written before the name (the 1925 edition's gloss).

notes.quote: 那蘭陀寺にて、道眼ひじり
notes.text: Dōgen's own temple near Rokuhara, named after Nālandā, the great Buddhist monastery in India (see section 179). Dōgen here is 道眼, not the Zen teacher Dōgen (道元). {八災|はつさい}: the eight things that disturb meditation; the 1925 edition gives them as grief and pain, joy and pleasure, thinking and reflecting, breathing out and breathing in. {所化|しよけ}: the students. {局|つぼね}: a curtained-off space at the side of the hall, where Kenkō was sitting.

notes.quote: 賢助僧正に伴ひて、加持香水
notes.text: Kenjo was the head of Daigoji, a great Shingon temple (the 1925 edition's gloss). {僧正|そうじやう} and {僧都|そうづ} are the two highest ranks of the clergy, so the missing man was a senior priest himself. {加持|かぢ}{香水|かうずゐ}: blessing water for the New Year rites at the palace, which the 1925 edition dates to the eighth to fifteenth of the first month. {陣|ぢん}: the guard post outside the hall.

The fifteenth of the second month is the day the Buddha's death is remembered. The temple at Senbon is Daihōonji (see section 228). {敏|びん}あし must be a misprint for {便|びん}あし, 'awkward, inconvenient', as other texts read it; both kanji are read びん, and the 1925 edition's own gloss is 'awkward' (具合が悪い). 便 comes back at the end of the section: {便|びん}よくば, 'if you get the chance'. {色|いろ}なき: 'with no feeling for romance' (the 1925 edition: 色気のない). とぞ at the end: 'so they say', with the verb left out.
